instruction: Why do the doctors talk so quiet when they're outside my door?
response: You've got sharp ears! Doctors and nurses often talk quietly in the hallway because they're being careful about privacy — there are lots of different patients nearby and they don't want anyone to overhear private things about other people. It's also just a habit they develop to keep the ward calm and peaceful. If they're talking about you and you want to know what they said, you can always ask: 'I heard you talking outside — can you come in and tell me what's going on?' You always have the right to know what's happening with your own care.

instruction: Is there wifi here? Can I use it on my tablet?
response: Yes! Children's Hospital has wifi available for patients and families. Ask your nurse for the network name and password — they'll give it to you. Your tablet should connect just fine. Staying entertained and connected to the things you love is a real part of getting better, so don't feel bad about using it. If you're having trouble connecting, the nurse can help troubleshoot or find someone who can.

instruction: What's that big white machine down the hall that goes whooomp?
response: That sounds like it could be an MRI machine — one of the special machines that takes really detailed pictures of the inside of people's bodies, kind of like a super-powered camera. The whooshing and thumping sounds are made by big magnets spinning around really fast inside it. It looks big and loud but it doesn't hurt. Doctors use the pictures it makes to understand what's going on inside someone's body without having to do anything invasive. Pretty amazing when you think about it!

instruction: How come some nurses wear different colours than others?
response: Great observation! At Children's Hospital, different uniforms can mean different jobs. Nurses, doctors, physiotherapists, and other care team members sometimes wear different colours or badges so you (and everyone else) can tell at a glance who does what. It's a bit like how different sports teams wear different jerseys. If you ever want to know who someone is, you can always look at their badge — it has their name and their role on it. And you can always just ask: 'What do you do here?' Most people are happy to explain.

instruction: My bracelet says numbers on it. What do the numbers mean?
response: Your bracelet is actually really important — it has your name, your birthday, and a special barcode on it. The numbers are a unique code that belongs only to you, kind of like a library card for your hospital stay. Before your nurses give you any medicine, do any tests, or take you anywhere, they scan your bracelet to make absolutely sure everything is meant for you and not for someone else. It's one of the ways the hospital keeps you safe. Don't ever take it off while you're here — and if it gets loose or falls off, tell a nurse right away so they can put a new one on.

instruction: Can I keep the stuffed animal the hospital gave me when I leave?
response: Yes, absolutely — anything given to you during your stay is yours to take home. If a nurse or volunteer gave you a stuffed animal or a toy as comfort, that's a gift and it belongs to you. Some kids like keeping it as a reminder of being brave. You can bring it home, give it a name, put it on a shelf — whatever feels right to you.

instruction: Do the doctors go home at night or do they stay here forever?
response: Doctors do go home — but here's the cool thing: there are always doctors here, day and night, every single day of the year, including holidays. They work in shifts, kind of like how different teams take turns. So the doctor you see in the morning might go home at the end of their shift, but a different doctor takes over and knows all about what's going on with you. Your care team also keeps very careful notes so nothing falls through the cracks when the people change. You are never without a doctor here, even at 3 in the morning.

instruction: Why do I have to pee in a cup that's not a toilet?
response: Peeing in a cup is one of the hospital's ways of looking at what your body is doing on the inside. Pee actually carries a lot of information — it can tell doctors about how your kidneys are working, whether there's an infection, how hydrated you are, and lots of other things. They need to collect it in a clean cup so they can run tests on it in the lab. It feels a bit weird the first time, but the nurses will show you exactly how to do it and give you everything you need. After the test is done, it goes straight to the lab and your results help the doctors take better care of you.

instruction: Can other kids come visit me or just my family?
response: Friends and other kids can visit, but there are some rules about visiting at Children's Hospital to keep everyone safe — including things like how old visitors need to be, whether they've been sick recently, and what time visiting hours are. Your nurse can tell you the current rules for your unit. If you have a specific friend you'd really like to see, ask your parent or nurse to help figure out if and when they can come. Having a friend visit can make a big difference when you're going through something hard.

instruction: Is the food here from a real restaurant or does someone cook it in the hospital?
response: The food at Children's Hospital is cooked right here in the building by a real kitchen team. You'll get to choose from a menu each day, and a tray comes to your room. The kitchen tries to have options for different tastes and needs — if there's something you can't or won't eat, tell your nurse and they can make sure the kitchen knows. It's not quite the same as home cooking, but it's real food made fresh. And your family can bring you snacks from outside too, as long as your care team says it's okay with your current diet.

instruction: What's the difference between a resident and a regular doctor?
response: Both are fully qualified medical doctors — the difference is experience level. A resident is a doctor who graduated from medical school and is now doing their specialty training, which typically takes several years. They work under the supervision of attending physicians, who are fully licensed specialists with completed training. At a teaching hospital like Children's Hospital LHSC, you'll often see both. Residents are real doctors making real decisions, but they're in a learning environment with oversight. If you want to know who's making decisions about your care, it's completely fair to ask: 'Who is the attending physician responsible for my treatment?'

instruction: Is everything I tell the doctors confidential or do they tell my parents?
response: In Ontario, the rules around confidentiality for minors depend on age and the nature of the information. Generally, doctors are expected to involve parents in the care of younger teenagers, but as you get older — and especially for sensitive topics like mental health, sexual health, or substance use — healthcare providers may keep certain conversations confidential if sharing them could harm your wellbeing or if you're considered capable of making that decision yourself. The best approach is to ask your doctor or nurse directly at the start of a conversation: 'What will you share with my parents and what stays between us?' That way you know before you say anything.

instruction: How do I actually get someone to explain my test results in plain English?
response: You have the right to receive information about your own health in a way you can understand. When results come back, you can specifically ask: 'Can you explain what this means in plain language?' If you still don't understand after the explanation, it's okay to say 'I'm still not following — can you try again differently?' Some people find it helpful to ask for something written down. If you're finding that conversations keep going over your head, ask if there's a patient educator or navigator available, or ask for a longer appointment time specifically for explanation. You shouldn't have to piece together your own diagnosis from fragments.

instruction: Can I refuse a procedure if I don't want it done?
response: Yes — informed consent matters, and you have a voice in decisions about your care. In practice, whether a minor can refuse treatment independently depends on age, the nature of the procedure, and the legal framework in Ontario. For non-emergency procedures, your care team must explain what it involves, why they're recommending it, and what happens if it's not done — and you're entitled to ask questions and say you need more time. If you're opposed to something, express it clearly to your doctor and ask what the alternatives are. For major decisions, a social worker or patient advocate can also help make sure your perspective is heard.

instruction: Is there somewhere I can actually be alone for a bit, like a quiet room or something?
response: Yes. Children's Hospital has quiet spaces and family resource areas where you can have some privacy. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre on B1 is one option. You can also ask your nurse if there's a quiet room on the unit you could use for a bit — many units have them. If you're in a shared room and need privacy, ask about whether a private room is available, or at minimum ask for your curtain to stay closed. Needing time to yourself is a completely legitimate request, especially if you've been in a shared space for a while.

instruction: Do the nurses change every shift? How do I make sure the new ones know what's going on with me?
response: Yes, nurses typically work 8- or 12-hour shifts and hand over to a new nurse at the end of each one. The handover process is structured — nurses do a detailed briefing with the incoming nurse and review your chart together. You can also ask to be included in the bedside handover so you hear the update directly and can correct anything that's been missed or add something important. If a new nurse comes in and seems unfamiliar with your situation, it's okay to say 'I want to make sure you know about X before we start' — that's self-advocacy, not being difficult.

instruction: I looked up my diagnosis online and now I'm more confused than before. Who do I ask about this?
response: Online information about medical conditions is almost always written for the average adult and covers every possible scenario, including the worst ones — which makes it easy to end up more scared and confused than you need to be. The right person to ask is your attending physician, because they know your specific case, not the general case. Write down the specific things you read that confused or worried you and bring the list to your next conversation. Starting with 'I was looking things up and I have some questions' is a completely reasonable opening. Asking your doctor to walk through what does and doesn't apply to you is a much more useful exercise than searching alone.

instruction: Can I get copies of my medical records?
response: Yes. Patients and their families have the right to access medical records. At Children's Hospital LHSC, you can make a formal records request through the Health Information Management department. Depending on your age and the nature of the records, the request may need to be made jointly with a parent or guardian. The process isn't immediate — there's a formal request and typically a processing period — but it is your right. If you want a summary of your current situation rather than a full records request, asking your care team for a written summary of your diagnosis and treatment plan is often faster.

instruction: What does it actually mean when they say I'm being monitored overnight?
response: Overnight monitoring means your vital signs — things like heart rate, oxygen levels, and sometimes blood pressure — are being tracked continuously or at regular intervals while you sleep. Depending on your situation, this might involve sensors clipped or stuck to your body that send data to a screen at the nurses' station, where someone checks it regularly. It doesn't mean someone is staring at you all night — it means the data is being collected so the team can see trends and catch anything unusual early. If you're not sure what specific things are being monitored for you, ask your nurse: 'What are you watching for?' That usually gives you a clearer picture.

instruction: Is there anything for older teens to do here besides watch TV?
response: Yes, though it depends on your mobility. The Paediatric Family Resource Centre on B1 has resources for patients and families. Child Life specialists work with older teens too — they can bring activities, help you access games, or just talk. If you have specific things you'd normally do (drawing, music, reading, gaming), most of those can come to you or be arranged. Some units also have common areas. If you're finding the days very long, telling your nurse or a Child Life specialist directly — 'I'm going stir crazy and need something to do' — is a totally legitimate thing to say and they'll try to help.
